newsitem.title: THAILAND: Suspense builds on eve of tight Thai poll race.
newsitem.headline: Suspense builds on eve of tight Thai poll race.

text.p: Politicians made final efforts to sway voters on the eve of Sunday's Thai election, seen by analysts as one of the closest ever and the most violent and dirty in two decades.

The Democrat Party led by former premier Chuan Leekpai and the New Aspiration Party (NAP) of outgoing Defence Minister Chavalit Yongchaiyudh were top contenders and running neck and neck in the fight for 393 seats in parliament.
Most opinion polls are divided and the two front-running parties themselves, which are expected to win around 125 seats each, predict that the margin will be thin, ranging from five to 10 seats.
The Democrats on Friday rejected an olive branch from NAP leader Chavalit who had proposed that the two key parties form a coalition government whatever the outcome of the polls.
"There must be someone to monitor the government and protect the interests of the people," Chuan said in Bangkok.
But Chavalit said in northeastern Udon that he would keep the proposal open despite the Democrats' rejection.

Traditionally, the party winning the most seats has the right to try to form a new government. But historically Thailand has had coalition governments because no single party has won enough seats to hold a parliamentary majority.
A total of 2,310 candidates from 13 parties is contesting the election, the country's second in 16 months after outgoing premier Banharn Silpa-archa set snap polls in late September.
Billions of baht have been used by politicians in this election which has been marred by the killing of at least eight people by gunmen. Dozens had also been attacked while campaigning, police said.
The Thai Farmers Research Centre estimated 20 billion baht ($800 million) would be spent by politicians on the election, 20 percent more than the amount spent in the last polls.
Rajabhat Institute of teachers' training said the poll was the most violent and dirty since the mid-1970s when student democracy groups toppled Thai military governments.
Pollwatch, the election watchdog, estimated that up to 30 billion baht had been spent on the election, including on vote-buying.
Police said two suspects were held and four million baht in fake banknotes intended for vote-buying seized in northeastern Ubon Rachatani.
Thailand's powerful military, which has launched 17 successful or attempted coups since 1932 when absolute monarchy ended, stressed its neutrality in the polls.
"I urged soldiers to exercise their right by voting for politicians of their choice and ordered them to be strictly neutral,"said army commander-in-chief, General Chetta Thanajaro said.

Thai business generally prefers a Democrat win because the party is known to have a strong economic team of qualified professionals and technocrats. The sector viewed the NAP as a party made up largely of defectors from other parties that might not cohesively manage the troubled economy.

Analysts said the Democrats needed to win at least 25 of the 37 seats in Bangkok to ensure an election victory. This was because they were expected to win almost the same number of seats as the NAP in rural areas.

Small parties were in big demand as potential coalition partners of the big two. The Chart Pattana Party of former premier Chatichai Choonhavan, which is expected to win over 50 seats, was being wooed by the NAP and Democrats.
